title: Bézout's Identity via Unimodular 2×2 Integer Matrices
description: Answers the open question from bezout-identity-oq-01: does the extended Euclidean algorithm correspond to unimodular 2×2 integer matrices? Yes. Each division step is left-multiplication by an elementary matrix eStep q = !![0,1;1,-q] of determinant -1 realising (a,b) ↦ (b, a % b); determinant is multiplicative so the composite stays unimodular; and the Bézout coefficient matrix !![gcdA, gcdB; -b/g, a/g] lies in SL₂(ℤ) (determinant 1) and carries the column (a,b)ᵀ to (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ. Main theorem: for (a,b) ≠ (0,0) there is a matrix in SL₂(ℤ) reducing (a,b)ᵀ to (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ — the matrix form of Bézout's identity. 9 theorems, 3 definitions, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: The connection between the Euclidean algorithm and 2×2 integer matrices is classical and underlies the theory of continued fractions and the modular group SL₂(ℤ). Each step of the Euclidean algorithm, replacing (a, b) by (b, a mod b), can be encoded as left-multiplication by an elementary matrix; the accumulated product of these matrices is unimodular (determinant ±1). This is the algebraic backbone of the reduction theory of binary quadratic forms (Gauss), the structure of SL₂(ℤ) as generated by the shear and swap matrices, and the matrix formulation of the continued-fraction expansion of a rational number. Bézout's identity gcd(a,b) = a·x + b·y (Étienne Bézout, 1779) states that the gcd is an integer linear combination; read as a matrix statement, it says the coefficient data assembles into an element of the special linear group that transforms the input column to (gcd, 0). The parent entry bezout-identity-oq-01 built a computable extended Euclidean algorithm extGcd; this entry answers its closing open question by exhibiting the algorithm's matrix incarnation.
overview.problemStatement: Show that the extended Euclidean algorithm corresponds to unimodular 2×2 integer matrices: exhibit an element of SL₂(ℤ) carrying (a, b)ᵀ to (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ, and identify the elementary matrices realising the individual division steps.
overview.text: For a quotient q, the elementary step matrix is eStep q = !![0, 1; 1, -q]. It has determinant -1 (eStep_det) and acts by eStep q *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![b, a - q·b]; taking q = a / b gives one Euclidean round eStep (a/b) *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![b, a % b] (eStep_euclid). Since det is multiplicative, det (M·N) = det M · det N, matrices of determinant ±1 are closed under multiplication (det_mul_unimodular), so the composite of the elementary steps of a full run is again unimodular. The endpoint of that run is the Bézout coefficient matrix bezoutMatrix a b = !![gcdA a b, gcdB a b; -b/g, a/g] where g = gcd a b. Writing g = a·gcdA + b·gcdB (Mathlib's Int.gcd_eq_gcd_ab) and clearing the exact divisions g ∣ a, g ∣ b shows det (bezoutMatrix a b) = 1 (bezoutMatrix_det) and bezoutMatrix a b *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![g, 0] (bezoutMatrix_mulVec). Packaging the matrix with its determinant proof gives bezoutSL a b : SL₂(ℤ), and the main theorem bezout_unimodular_reduction states ∃ M : SL₂(ℤ), M *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![gcd a b, 0].
overview.proofStrategy: Purely algebraic, no induction on the algorithm. Determinants of 2×2 literals are computed by Matrix.det_fin_two_of; the action of a 2×2 matrix on a length-2 column is computed once and for all by a helper mulVec_two. The determinant and the vanishing second component both reduce to identities of the form g·(expression) = g·(target), settled by clearing g ∣ a and g ∣ b via Int.ediv_mul_cancel and cancelling the nonzero g with mul_left_cancel₀; the first component is exactly Bézout's identity, closed by linear_combination against Int.gcd_eq_gcd_ab.
keyInsights: The extended Euclidean algorithm is precisely an SL₂(ℤ) row-reduction: the sequence of elementary matrices eStep q multiplies to a unimodular matrix carrying (a,b)ᵀ to (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ. Bézout's coefficients are literally the top row of that matrix.

Determinant 1 (rather than merely ±1) is forced by the specific second row (-b/g, a/g): det = gcdA·(a/g) + gcdB·(b/g), and multiplying through by g recovers a·gcdA + b·gcdB = g, so det = 1 after cancelling the nonzero g.

The exact integer divisions a/g and b/g are legitimate because g = gcd a b divides both a and b; Int.ediv_mul_cancel turns a/g·g back into a, which is the only arithmetic fact needed to clear denominators.

The elementary step eStep q = !![0,1;1,-q] has determinant -1, not +1, so a single step is orientation-reversing; unimodularity (closure under multiplication) is what guarantees the full run lands in the determinant-±1 subgroup, and the specific Bézout endpoint has determinant exactly +1.

The proof is native_decide-free and axiom-free: the concrete example gcd 12 18 = 6 is discharged by kernel decide, and the general theorems by algebraic tactics, so the entry is genuinely verified rather than axiomatized.
prerequisites: Bézout coefficients in Mathlib: Int.gcdA, Int.gcdB, Int.gcd_eq_gcd_ab
2×2 determinants and matrix–vector products: Matrix.det_fin_two_of, Matrix.det_mul, dotProduct, Fin.sum_univ_two
The special linear group Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ

conclusion.summary: The extended Euclidean algorithm is the action of SL₂(ℤ) on integer columns: elementary step matrices eStep q (det -1) realise (a,b) ↦ (b, a % b), and the Bézout coefficient matrix !![gcdA,gcdB;-b/g,a/g] lies in SL₂(ℤ) and reduces (a,b)ᵀ to (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ. 9 theorems, 3 definitions, 0 axioms, 0 sorries, 175 lines.
conclusion.implications: This gives the structural / group-theoretic reading of Bézout's identity that the computable parent (bezout-identity-oq-01) left open: the Bézout coefficients are the top row of an explicit SL₂(ℤ) matrix. The same elementary matrices generate the modular group and drive continued-fraction and quadratic-form reduction, so the result is the entry point to those theories.
openQuestions: Prove that bezoutMatrix a b is literally the product of the elementary matrices eStep qᵢ for the successive quotients qᵢ of the Euclidean algorithm (reconstruct the accumulated product, not just its endpoint).
Generalise to a Euclidean domain: for k[X] exhibit the analogous unimodular 2×2 matrix over k[X] reducing (a, b) to (gcd a b, 0).

mainTheorems.name: bezout_unimodular_reduction
mainTheorems.description: For (a,b) ≠ (0,0) there exists M ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with M *ᵥ (a,b)ᵀ = (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ — the matrix form of Bézout's identity.

mainTheorems.name: bezoutMatrix_det
mainTheorems.description: The Bézout coefficient matrix !![gcdA,gcdB;-b/g,a/g] has determinant 1, i.e. lies in SL₂(ℤ). Proved by multiplying through by g and reducing to a·gcdA + b·gcdB = g.

mainTheorems.name: bezoutMatrix_mulVec
mainTheorems.description: The Bézout matrix carries (a,b)ᵀ to (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ: the first component is Bézout's identity, the second vanishes after clearing the exact divisions g ∣ a, g ∣ b.

mainTheorems.name: eStep_euclid
mainTheorems.description: With the true quotient q = a / b, the elementary matrix eStep q realises one Euclidean round: eStep (a/b) *ᵥ (a,b)ᵀ = (b, a % b)ᵀ.

mainTheorems.name: det_mul_unimodular
mainTheorems.description: Unimodular (determinant ±1) integer matrices are closed under multiplication, so composites of elementary Euclidean steps stay unimodular.

sections.title: Module Header and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Imports Mathlib. Documents the open question (does extGcd correspond to unimodular 2×2 matrices?) and the four-part answer: elementary steps are unimodular, unimodularity is preserved under multiplication, the Bézout matrix lands in SL₂(ℤ), and reduces (a,b)ᵀ to (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ.

sections.title: Elementary Euclidean-Step Matrices
sections.summary: Defines eStep q = !![0,1;1,-q]. eStep_det proves determinant -1; eStep_apply computes its action (a,b) ↦ (b, a - q·b); eStep_euclid specialises to q = a/b giving one Euclidean round (a,b) ↦ (b, a % b) via Int.emod_def.

sections.title: Closure of Unimodular Matrices
sections.summary: det_mul_unimodular: determinant is multiplicative (Matrix.det_mul), so matrices of determinant ±1 are closed under multiplication. mulVec_two computes the action of a general 2×2 matrix on a length-2 column.

sections.title: The Bézout Coefficient Matrix
sections.summary: Defines bezoutMatrix a b = !![gcdA,gcdB;-b/g,a/g] with g = gcd a b. gcd_cast_ne_zero handles nonvanishing of g; bezoutMatrix_det proves determinant 1 by multiplying through by g and applying Bézout's identity plus the exact divisions g ∣ a, g ∣ b.

sections.title: Reduction of the Input Column
sections.summary: bezoutMatrix_mulVec proves bezoutMatrix a b *ᵥ (a,b)ᵀ = (gcd a b, 0)ᵀ: entry 0 is Bézout's identity (linear_combination), entry 1 vanishes after clearing g ∣ a, g ∣ b and cancelling the nonzero g.

sections.title: Membership in SL₂(ℤ) and Main Theorem
sections.summary: bezoutSL packages the Bézout matrix with its determinant-1 proof as an element of Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ; bezout_unimodular_reduction states the matrix form of Bézout's identity.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.summary: A concrete Euclidean step (17,5) ↦ (5, 17 % 5) via eStep, and a concrete unimodular reduction sending (12,18)ᵀ to (6,0)ᵀ with gcd 12 18 = 6 checked by kernel decide.
